```{r setup}
library(BetaVolume)
```

This vignette walks through the geometric approach to beta diversity of
Song et al. (2025, *Ecological Monographs* 95:e70008,
<https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.70008>) and reproduces the worked examples of the
paper with BetaVolume.

## The idea: beta diversity as a hypervolume

Consider two species, A and B. Metacommunity I has a community with only A
and a community with only B. Metacommunity II has, in addition, a community
with both species (Fig. 1 of the paper). Classic measures say that
metacommunity I is *more* diverse: for Whittaker's multiplicative beta,
$\beta = \gamma / \bar\alpha$ is $2/1 = 2$ for I but $2/(4/3) = 1.5$ for II.
Adding a distinct, species-rich community *decreases* beta diversity.

The geometric approach instead writes the metacommunity as a matrix, with
communities in rows and species in columns:

```{r}
meta_I <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 1))
meta_II <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 1), c(1, 1))
colnames(meta_I) <- colnames(meta_II) <- c("A", "B")
meta_II
```

Each row is a point in a space with one axis per species. Together with the
origin (an empty community must not change beta diversity), the points span a
convex polytope $P$. For metacommunity I this is a triangle of area 1/2. For
metacommunity II it is the unit square, area 1. Beta diversity is the rescaled
hypervolume

$$\beta_{vol} = d \times \mathrm{vol}(P)^{1/d}, \qquad d = \min(\gamma, N),$$

where $\gamma$ is the number of species and $N$ the number of communities. It
is an effective number of communities between 0 (all communities identical)
and $d$:

```{r}
betavolume(meta_I) # 2 * sqrt(1/2)
betavolume(meta_II) # 2 * sqrt(1)
```

```{r fig1, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:2) {
  m <- list(meta_I, meta_II)[[k]]
  pts <- rbind(m, 0)
  hull <- chull(pts)
  plot(pts, xlim = c(-0.1, 1.2), ylim = c(-0.1, 1.2), asp = 1, pch = 19,
       col = c(rep("steelblue", nrow(m)), "firebrick"),
       xlab = "Species A", ylab = "Species B",
       main = sprintf("Metacommunity %s: beta = %.2f", c("I", "II")[k], betavolume(m)))
  polygon(pts[hull, ], col = adjustcolor("forestgreen", 0.3), border = "forestgreen")
}
par(op)
```

The matrix may be given either way round. The smaller dimension always
defines the axes, and `betavolume(t(meta_II))` is identical.

### All metacommunities with three species

With three species there are $2^3 - 1 = 7$ non-empty compositions. Below we
compute $\beta_{vol}$ for every metacommunity built from a subset of these
compositions (cf. Fig. 2 of the paper). Beta diversity increases, sublinearly,
with the number of unique compositions and reaches its maximum, 3, only when
all seven are present. At a given number of compositions, the most distinct
compositions give the highest beta diversity.

```{r fig2}
comps <- as.matrix(expand.grid(A = 0:1, B = 0:1, C = 0:1))[-1, ]
subsets <- unlist(lapply(1:7, function(k) combn(7, k, simplify = FALSE)),
                  recursive = FALSE)
beta <- vapply(subsets, function(s) {
  # repeat rows so that N >= gamma: duplicated compositions do not change P
  betavolume(comps[rep(s, length.out = max(3, length(s))), , drop = FALSE])
}, numeric(1))
n_unique <- lengths(subsets)
plot(jitter(n_unique, 0.3), beta, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4),
     xlab = "Number of unique community compositions",
     ylab = expression(beta[vol]))
tapply(beta, n_unique, max)
```

## Presence/absence data: weighting duplicated compositions

With presence/absence data many communities share the same composition and
map to the same point, so the plain hypervolume ignores how often each
composition occurs. With `weights = TRUE`, BetaVolume uses the weighted
embedding of Eq. 5 of the paper. Each unique composition $k$ that occurs
$n_k$ times among $N$ communities is scaled by $m\,n_k/N$, where $m$ is the
number of unique compositions. This is the example of Fig. 4:

```{r}
fig4 <- rbind(
  c(1, 0),
  c(0, 1), c(0, 1),
  c(1, 1), c(1, 1), c(1, 1)
)
colnames(fig4) <- c("A", "B")
preprocess_meta_composition(fig4, weights = TRUE)
betavolume(fig4) # duplicates ignored
betavolume(fig4, weights = TRUE) # duplicates weighted
```

The weights average to one over the unique compositions, so metacommunities
without duplicates are unaffected.

**Note for users of BetaVolume 0.1.0.** Older versions used the weights
$N n_k / \sum_l n_l^2$, which are proportional to (but smaller than) the
weights of Eq. 5. They give the same contributions (below) but smaller
`betavolume(weights = TRUE)` values. Use `weight_scheme = "legacy"` to
reproduce old results:

```{r}
betavolume(fig4, weights = TRUE, weight_scheme = "legacy")
```

## Which communities matter? Contributions to beta diversity

The contribution of a community is the normalised loss of beta diversity when
it is removed (Eq. 7):

$$C_i = \frac{\mathrm{vol}(P_0)^{1/d} - \mathrm{vol}(P_{\setminus i})^{1/d}}
{\sum_j \left(\mathrm{vol}(P_0)^{1/d} - \mathrm{vol}(P_{\setminus j})^{1/d}\right)}.$$

For the weighted metacommunity of Fig. 4 we recover the values of Fig. 6
(0.16, 0.37 and 0.47). With `weights = TRUE`, each unique composition is
one unit, labelled by the communities that share it:

```{r}
round(disentangle_individual_contribution(fig4, weights = TRUE), 3)
```

With the exact method, contributions are never negative: only communities on
the boundary of the hull contribute. In the example data set (37 species in
10 plots of A. H. Gentry's forest transect data) the plots are the axes, so
the contributions are those of species:

```{r}
dim(example_meta_composition)
contrib <- disentangle_individual_contribution(example_meta_composition)
round(head(sort(contrib, decreasing = TRUE), 5), 3)
sum(contrib > 0) # species on the boundary of the hull
```

With `weights = TRUE`, species with identical occurrence patterns are merged
into one weighted point and receive a single, joint contribution, labelled by
all the species that share it.

## Species similarity and functional complementarity

Following Leinster & Cobbold (2012), a similarity matrix $S$ ($s_{ij} = 0$:
totally dissimilar, $s_{ij} = 1$: identical) turns the orthogonal species axes
into the columns of $S$. The hypervolume is then rescaled by the normalised
solid angle $\Omega(S)$ of the cone spanned by the new axes (Eqs. 8 and 9).
`get_compressed_angle()` returns the factor $\Omega(S)^{1/d}$ to pass to
`betavolume()`:

```{r}
S_similar <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2) # Fig. 7C
S_complementary <- matrix(c(1, -0.5, -0.5, 1), 2) # Fig. 7D

get_compressed_angle(diag(2)) # dissimilar species: unchanged
get_compressed_angle(matrix(1, 2, 2)) # identical species: no beta diversity
get_compressed_angle(S_similar) # similarity shrinks
get_compressed_angle(S_complementary) # complementarity expands

betavolume(meta_II, compressed_angle = get_compressed_angle(S_similar))
```

For up to three species the solid angle has a closed form. Beyond that it is
an orthant probability of a multivariate normal distribution, estimated by
quasi-Monte Carlo (call `set.seed()` for reproducibility).

## Temporal change as hypervolume overlap

The change of a metacommunity from time $t$ to $t+1$ is measured by the
overlap of the two embeddings (Eq. 6):
$\beta_{t\to t+1} = \left(\mathrm{vol}(P_{t+1}\cap P_t)/\mathrm{vol}(P_t)\right)^{1/d}$.
This is the example of Fig. 5:

```{r}
t0 <- rbind(c(0, 1), c(1, 1)) # community 1 = {B}, community 2 = {A, B}
t1 <- rbind(c(0, 1), c(1, 0)) # community 2 loses B: asynchronous change
t2 <- rbind(c(1, 0), c(0, 1)) # the communities swap: synchronous change

beta_temporal_overlap(t0, t1)
beta_temporal_overlap(t1, t2) # identical shapes
beta_temporal_overlap(t1, t2, oriented = TRUE) # but opposite orientation
```

With `oriented = TRUE` the embedding is oriented from the origin to community
1, to community 2, and so on. Opposite orientations reveal synchronous changes
(values above 1) that the unoriented overlap cannot see. The orientation is
defined when each embedding is a simplex ($d$ communities in $d$
dimensions).

## Large metacommunities

Exact convex hulls become expensive beyond roughly 10 to 15 dimensions. By
default, `betavolume()` switches to the hyper-normal approximation when the
embedding dimension exceeds `dim_threshold = 10`:

$$\beta \approx 4\, d\, \det(\Sigma)^{1/d},$$

where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the embedded points (including
the origin). The constant $4 = 1/\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2))$ puts it
on the scale of $\beta_{vol}$. A presence/absence metacommunity containing all
$2^d$ compositions gets $\beta \approx d$:

```{r}
all_10 <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(0:1), 10)))
betavolume(all_10, hypervolume_method = "hyper_normal")
```

The approximation handles thousands of species or sites and accepts sparse
matrices from the **Matrix** package without densifying them:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
big <- Matrix::rsparsematrix(5000, 300, density = 0.02,
                             rand.x = function(n) rep(1, n))
system.time(b <- betavolume(big))
b
```

Note that the hyper-normal estimator scales like a variance: multiplying
abundances by $c$ multiplies it by $c^2$, whereas $\beta_{vol}$ is multiplied
by $c$. Compare metacommunities with a single method and the same
normalisation of abundances.

## Julia

The `julia/` folder of the GitHub repository contains **BetaVolume.jl**, a
Julia implementation of the same functions, cross-validated against this
package, for very large analyses.

## References

Song, C., Lu, M., Bennett, J. R., Gilbert, B., Fortin, M.-J., & Gonzalez, A.
(2025). A geometric approach to beta diversity. *Ecological Monographs*,
95(1), e70008. <https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.70008>

Leinster, T., & Cobbold, C. A. (2012). Measuring diversity: the importance of
species similarity. *Ecology*, 93(3), 477–489.
<https://doi.org/10.1890/10-2402.1>
